sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe electronic claim submission, including the standardized 837 transaction and required data elements.
- Explain the role of clearinghouses, electronic acknowledgments, and claim status inquiry in the submission process.
- Distinguish between claim rejections and denials and describe the appropriate response to each.
- Explain timely-filing requirements and the assistant's role in tracking and protecting filing deadlines.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An electronic claim is like sending a bill through the computer instead of mailing a paper letter — it uses a special shared code so the insurance company's computer can read it instantly.

### Question 2

The 837P is like the standard claim "envelope" that carries a doctor's bill; different letters after 837 are for hospitals (I) and dentists (D).

### Question 3

Hospitals use the "I" (institutional) version, doctor offices use "P" (professional), and dentists use "D" — like different sizes of the same box.

### Question 4

HIPAA made a common language for claims so any doctor's computer can talk to any insurance computer, like everyone agreeing to use the same alphabet.

### Question 5

Sending a bill by computer is like emailing instead of mailing a letter — it gets there instantly and tells you right away if something is wrong.

### Question 6

The claim is like a detailed receipt: who the patient is, what was done, why (the diagnosis), and how much it costs.

### Question 7

A clean claim is like turning in homework with every answer filled in and no smudges — it can be graded right away.

### Question 8

A companion guide is like a teacher's specific instructions for filling out a form, on top of the general rules everyone follows.

### Question 9

Before two computers can exchange bills, both sides have to "sign up" and agree how to talk — like setting up a new account before you can send messages.

### Question 10

A trading partner agreement is like a handshake and a written promise about how two companies will share bills electronically.

### Question 11

Direct submission is like handing a letter straight to one friend instead of going through a mailroom that sorts lots of letters.

### Question 12

Batching is like mailing a whole stack of letters in one envelope instead of sending them one at a time.

### Question 13

Computers need everything in the same code, like a cashier needs barcodes instead of handwriting, so the machine can read it fast.

### Question 14

The 837 is built like a filing cabinet with labeled drawers — each drawer holds one kind of information in the same order every time.

### Question 15

The NPI is like a provider's official ID number that every insurance computer recognizes.

### Question 16

A rejection is like a bounced email — it never got delivered because something about the address or format was wrong.

### Question 17

A clearinghouse is like a post office for electronic bills: it checks the address, tidies the envelope, and sends each bill to the right insurance company.

### Question 18

Instead of wiring the office computer to every insurance company one by one, the clearinghouse is one big hub that connects to all of them for you.

### Question 19

A scrubber is like a spell-checker for bills — it catches mistakes so you can fix them before you hit send.

### Question 20

The clearinghouse is like a translator who takes your message and says it in whatever language each insurance company speaks.

### Question 21

The clearinghouse sends back a receipt that says "got it" or "needs fixing," like a delivery confirmation for your bill.

### Question 22

Once the bill checks out, the clearinghouse delivers it to the insurance company to be reviewed and paid.

### Question 23

The clearinghouse is the mail sorter, not the judge — the insurance company is the one that decides and pays.

### Question 24

Pick a clearinghouse the way you pick a phone service: it has to work with your phone and reach the people you call.

### Question 25

The 999/277CA is like a "message received" or "message failed" reply that comes back after you send a bill.

### Question 26

The 270/271 is like calling ahead to ask, "Is this patient's insurance card good?" before the appointment.

### Question 27

The 835 is the insurance company's "receipt and explanation" showing what they paid and why, sent electronically.

### Question 28

EFT is like a direct deposit — the money goes straight into the bank account instead of a check arriving in the mail.

### Question 29

A rejection is a "return to sender" — the bill never got inside, so you fix the mistake and send it again.

### Question 30

The 276/277 is like calling a package hotline and asking, "Where is my package?" — and getting a tracking update.

### Question 31

Besides the computer "tracking number," offices can check a claim by looking it up on the insurance website or calling them.

### Question 32

"Finalized" is like a package marked "delivered" — the insurance company is done reviewing that bill.

### Question 33

If a bill is still "being worked on," you write it down and check again later — you don't send it twice or give up.

### Question 34

Writing down every call is like keeping a journal of the package search — so anyone can see exactly what you already tried.

### Question 35

"More information needed" is like the insurance company saying, "We got your bill, but we need one more paper to finish."

### Question 36

If your package hasn't arrived, you check the tracking number first — you don't just blame the recipient or give up.

### Question 37

A rejection is "returned to sender, never opened"; a denial is "opened, read, and answered no."

### Question 38

A typo in a code is like a wrong address on a letter — it bounces back before anyone opens it.

### Question 39

The insurance company opened the bill, read it, and said, "This kind of service isn't covered" — that's a denial.

### Question 40

Passing front-end edits is like getting through the door — you still have to be reviewed inside before anything is decided.

### Question 41

The insurance company looked at the bill and said the service wasn't needed — that decision is a denial, not a bounced envelope.

### Question 42

If your letter bounced back for a bad address, you fix the address and mail it again — you don't have to file a formal complaint.

### Question 43

If the insurance company says no, you read why, then fix it or ask them to reconsider — you don't throw it away or resend it unchanged.

### Question 44

"Accepted" means the letter was received and opened — not that the answer will be yes.

### Question 45

Sending the same bill twice makes the insurance computer think it already handled it, so it says "already got this one."

### Question 46

Missing ID number = bounced before opening; coverage and authorization problems = decided after opening.

### Question 47

Timely filing is like a due date for turning in the bill — send it too late and the insurance company can refuse it.

### Question 48

Different insurance companies have different due dates, like different teachers with different homework deadlines — you have to track each one.

### Question 49

Turn in the bill after the due date and the insurance company can say "too late" and refuse to pay.

### Question 50

Keep the "delivery receipt" with the date stamp — that's how you prove you turned it in on time.

### Question 51

Turn things in early and keep a checklist, like a student who tracks every due date instead of cramming at the end.

### Question 52

Fixing a typo and resending is quick; arguing about whether a service was covered takes a formal request to reconsider.

### Question 53

If the insurance company requires an "okay in advance" and the office forgot to ask, they can refuse to pay afterward.

### Question 54

When you disagree with a "no," you gather your evidence and formally ask them to look again — you don't just resend the same thing.

### Question 55

Telling the patient "we just need to fix a typo" versus "the insurance won't cover this" are two very different messages, and they deserve the right one.

### Question 56

The insurance company agreed to pay a set price and adjusted the rest — that's normal, not a mistake.

### Question 57

It's a straight line: send the bill, get the "received" check, have it reviewed, then get the answer (paid or not).

### Question 58

If a bill bounces back, you fix it and resend quickly — and if you're stuck, you ask the billing expert, because the clock is ticking.

### Question 59

Count 180 days on the calendar from the visit date — that's the last day to turn the bill in.

### Question 60

Medicare gives a full year — like a school project due at the end of the year — but it still must be turned in on time.

### Question 61

When you turn in a corrected version, the due date might change, so you check that payer's rule instead of assuming it's the same.

### Question 62

DDE is like typing your order directly into a website form instead of uploading a big file.

### Question 63

The provider portal is like an online account page where you can look up what happened to each bill.

### Question 64

You need your login and the right "tracking number" to look up a bill — just like checking a bank account.

### Question 65

Explain what the paperwork says in simple words, and if it's a medical question you can't answer, hand it to the expert.

### Question 66

You can fix a typo, but you can never change the facts to make the bill pass — that's cheating the system.

### Question 67

If you missed the due date, you ask if there's a late excuse that's true — you never change the date to make it look on time.

### Question 68

The assistant double-checks the "address and name" on every bill so it doesn't bounce back — but the doctor's team picks the codes.

### Question 69

Checking the insurance card is real and active before billing is like checking the address before you mail a letter.

### Question 70

You have the dated delivery receipt — show it to the insurance company to prove you mailed it on time.

### Question 71

The assistant is the careful helper who checks the form; the doctor's team is the one who decides the medical parts.

### Question 72

When you're not sure of the rule, ask the person in charge instead of guessing — that's the safe move.

### Question 73

The kind of bill (doctor's office vs. hospital) picks the right envelope, not how much it costs.

### Question 74

If they ask for one more paper, you gather what truly exists and send it safely — you never make one up.

### Question 75

You only look up bills for patients you're actually helping — never for curiosity, because that's private information.

### Question 76

If the tracking number comes up empty, first check whether you really sent it, then work with the insurance company to find it.

### Question 77

The bill that's been sitting unsent for months is the one in danger of being "too late."

### Question 78

Those fields are the "To:" address on the bill's envelope so it reaches the right insurance company.

### Question 79

Sometimes the "sent" receipt and the "received" record don't match — you investigate with both companies to find where it got stuck.

### Question 80

Fix a bill using the real paperwork, not your memory or what would pay more.

### Question 81

Adjudication is the judge's decision on the bill; the front-end is just the door check.

### Question 82

If the due date changes, you update your calendar and tell everyone — you don't keep using the old date.

### Question 83

Filling in a missing birthday and resending is an easy fix — the harder ones need the experts.

### Question 84

Match the "sent" list against the "answered" list to find bills that got lost in between.

### Question 85

When you're new and unsure, you follow the instructions and ask for help — that's the safe and smart way to learn.
